paragraphs: This paper uses an analogy with evolutionary algorithms to rethink the Vision Transformer. The authors argue that the two approaches share a mathematical representation, giving them a way to interpret transformer operations through ideas from biological evolution. They use this connection as a basis for designing a more efficient sequence model called EAT.

The architectural change draws on the idea of a dynamic local population in an evolutionary algorithm. Task-specific heads let the resulting model serve different purposes. The authors also introduce a spatial-filling curve to arrange image data into a sequence. Together, these choices separate the adaptation of data formats from the core network architecture, supporting a unified framework for multimodal tasks.

On ImageNet classification, the paper reports state-of-the-art results relative to recent vision transformers, with fewer parameters and higher throughput. It also evaluates text-based image retrieval, reporting a 3.7-point rank-1 improvement over the baseline on CSS. These findings support the proposed architecture's efficiency and usefulness across the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2021-analogous-to-evolutionary-a.tldr: EAT uses an evolutionary-algorithm analogy to build an efficient sequence architecture for image and multimodal tasks.

paragraphs: Artistic style transfer can produce unwanted repetition and colors that do not fit together. This paper addresses those artifacts by combining information from the chosen style image with information learned from a large style dataset. The approach aims to retain the particular appearance of the reference while producing more harmonious results.

The reference image supplies internal statistics that determine colors and texture patterns. External learning supplies broader style information intended to reflect human perceptions of style. The method also compares stylized outputs with one another, extending the usual relationships between an output and its content or style reference.

Two contrastive losses implement these comparisons. They bring representations of stylizations closer when the outputs share content or style, and separate them otherwise. This gives training a way to encourage consistency across related outputs. Experiments report more visually harmonious and satisfying images, along with better stability and consistency in rendered video clips. The stated benefits therefore concern both individual image appearance and coherence across video.
neurips-2021-artistic-style-transfer-wit.tldr: The method combines reference-image statistics, learned style knowledge, and contrastive losses to improve stylized images and video consistency.

paragraphs: Bayesian decision algorithms use prior beliefs to guide exploration, but those beliefs can be wrong. This paper quantifies how much that mismatch can affect Thompson sampling. It compares the expected accumulated reward obtained with a misspecified prior against the reward obtained with a correctly specified one.

The reward difference is bounded by a quantity scaling roughly as H squared times epsilon, up to logarithmic factors. Here H is the learning horizon, and epsilon measures total-variation distance between the priors. The result requires no parametric form for the prior. For bounded-support priors, the bound does not depend on the action space's size or structure, and the authors establish worst-case tightness up to universal constants.

The sensitivity analysis also yields probabilistic learning guarantees for Bayesian meta-learning. Extensions cover a broader family of decision algorithms, including a Monte Carlo knowledge-gradient implementation, and Bayesian partially observable decision processes. Simulations illustrate how prior mismatch and one-step look-ahead influence meta-learning convergence with structured and correlated priors.
neurips-2021-bayesian-decision-making-un.tldr: The paper bounds how prior misspecification affects Bayesian decision-making and uses that analysis to establish meta-learning guarantees.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks incorporate physical equations as penalties in the training objective. This paper investigates why that approach can fail even when a problem is only somewhat more complex than the simple examples it handles successfully. The analysis covers differential equations involving convection, reaction, and diffusion.

The authors provide evidence that penalties built from differential operators can make optimization poorly conditioned. In the cases studied, the difficulty comes from the training landscape created by the formulation, rather than insufficient expressive power in the network. A network may be capable of representing the relevant physical behavior while training still struggles to find it.

The paper proposes two promising remedies. Curriculum regularization begins with a simpler equation-based penalty and increases its complexity during training. A sequence-to-sequence formulation breaks up prediction instead of fitting the entire space-time solution at once. Extensive tests report errors up to one or two orders of magnitude lower than regular PINN training. These results highlight training formulation as a practical route to addressing the identified failures.
neurips-2021-characterizing-possible-fai.tldr: The paper traces possible PINN failures to difficult optimization and tests two training formulations that substantially reduce error.

paragraphs: Coordinated Proximal Policy Optimization extends PPO to settings where multiple agents learn together. Its central idea is to coordinate how far agents move during policy updates. This makes the adaptation of update step sizes a joint concern when several policies change concurrently.

The authors first construct a theoretically grounded joint objective and prove monotonic policy improvement when optimizing it. They then use approximations to derive a simpler optimization objective. The distinction matters: the improvement theorem concerns the theoretical objective, while the simplified objective is the practical form derived from it. The authors interpret this simplified form as dynamically assigning credit among agents, helping alleviate high variance during simultaneous policy updates.

Experiments include cooperative matrix games and StarCraft II micromanagement tasks. CoPPO outperforms several strong baselines and is competitive with MAPPO in these settings. The results support coordinated updates as a useful design for cooperative multi-agent learning, alongside a theoretical account of why optimizing a suitable joint objective can improve policies.
neurips-2021-coordinated-proximal-policy.tldr: CoPPO coordinates agents' policy-update sizes, combining a joint improvement analysis with competitive cooperative multi-agent results.

paragraphs: Differentially private stochastic gradient descent can impose a substantial runtime cost, sometimes reaching two orders of magnitude above ordinary training. This paper studies how much of that overhead can be reduced through implementation choices. Its focus is on executing private training efficiently using capabilities already available in machine-learning frameworks.

The approach combines vectorization, just-in-time compilation, and static graph optimization. These mechanisms let the software express and optimize computation more effectively. The authors implement the approach in JAX using its support for the XLA compiler. They also rebuild core components of TensorFlow Privacy, introducing more effective vectorization and XLA compilation into that framework.

The paper reports substantial runtime and memory improvements over previous TensorFlow Privacy releases and speedups of up to 50 times compared with the best alternatives. In many evaluated cases, runtime nearly matches the best non-private training times. These findings show that implementation overhead can account for a large, reducible part of the cost of private training, making compiler and framework design practically important.
neurips-2021-enabling-fast-differentiall.tldr: Vectorization and compiler optimizations greatly accelerate private SGD, in many cases bringing runtime close to non-private training.

paragraphs: Neuro-symbolic learning combines perception from raw inputs with logical background knowledge. Abductive reasoning helps reconcile the two by revising perceived facts that conflict with that knowledge. Earlier approaches depend on an initialized perception model that already distinguishes inputs, which can require substantial pretraining when classification is difficult.

This paper changes what guides the abductive search. Instead of relying on the perceptual network's output information, it uses similarities between samples. The resulting method, ABductive Learning with Similarity, or ABLSim, makes those relationships the basis for seeking consistency with symbolic knowledge. This directly addresses the dependence on a perception model that is already good at separating instances.

The authors apply ABLSim to difficult neuro-symbolic learning tasks. Experiments report substantially higher efficiency than state-of-the-art neuro-symbolic methods, together with better performance using less labeled data and weaker domain knowledge. The findings support sample similarity as a useful source of guidance when combining learned perception and reasoning, particularly where obtaining a strong initial classifier is burdensome.
neurips-2021-fast-abductive-learning-by-.tldr: ABLSim guides abductive reasoning with sample similarity, improving efficiency and performance with less supervision in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Contextual bandits learn personalized decisions from information about individuals and the outcomes of previous choices. That creates a privacy challenge when a server should not see users' private data. This paper develops algorithms for stochastic generalized linear bandits under local differential privacy, which places privacy protection at the user side of the interaction.

The main construction uses a stochastic-gradient estimator together with an update mechanism designed to ensure local privacy. The authors exploit the flexibility of stochastic gradient descent for generalized linear bandits and provide a theoretical treatment of its use in this setting. They also introduce an estimator and update mechanism based on ordinary least squares for the linear-bandit case.

The paper states that its algorithms achieve the same regret bound as in non-private settings. Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets report consistently strong performance under local privacy constraints with reasonably small epsilon and delta parameters. Together, the theory and experiments support effective personalized learning within the privacy framework studied.
neurips-2021-generalized-linear-bandits-.tldr: The paper develops locally private generalized linear bandit algorithms with stated regret bounds matching the non-private setting.

paragraphs: Joint probabilities of potential outcomes describe how outcomes under different causal circumstances relate to one another. They support questions about whether a cause was necessary, sufficient, or both. Identifying these probabilities also identifies causal risk, but identifying causal risk alone does not generally recover the joint probabilities.

These quantities cannot be identified without assumptions. Existing approaches use conditions such as monotonicity, independence between potential outcomes, or particular cause-effect relationships. This paper proposes two alternative types of identification conditions based on covariate information. The contribution is a different route to identification that avoids those listed assumptions while still requiring the proposed conditions.

Identification also creates an estimation challenge: under the new conditions, the problem involves singular statistical models, for which standard estimation methods do not apply. The authors develop an estimator using the augmented Lagrangian method and establish its asymptotic normality. The work therefore addresses both when the causal quantities can be recovered and how to estimate them in the resulting nonstandard statistical setting.
neurips-2021-identification-and-estimati.tldr: The paper introduces covariate-based identification conditions for joint potential outcomes and an estimator suited to the resulting singular models.

paragraphs: Traditional software allows intermediate variables to be traced back to inputs and components to be composed into larger programs. This paper takes a step toward related capabilities in neural networks. Its Decodable Neural Network, or DecNN, jointly trains a generative model that constrains internal activations to decode back into inputs.

That connection between representations and inputs enables a form of recursive composition. A DecNN can be composed with itself to produce an ensemble-like model with uncertainty. The design makes uncertainty available through this composition, linking the proposed architectural constraint to practical ways of examining a network's predictions.

Experiments apply the uncertainty to detecting out-of-distribution inputs, detecting adversarial examples, and calibration, while matching standard neural networks in accuracy. The authors also combine DecNN with pretrained models and report promising results for regularizing networks away from using protected features. These findings present decoding as a useful route toward limited compositional capabilities, with demonstrated applications to uncertainty and an exploratory application to feature use.
neurips-2021-improving-compositionality-.tldr: DecNN makes internal representations decodable to inputs, enabling recursive composition and useful uncertainty estimates while retaining classification accuracy.

paragraphs: Dropout regularizes a neural network within a predetermined backbone, but deep models can still assign high confidence to incorrect predictions. This paper proposes learning network depth and dropout together through Bayesian model selection. The aim is to let the data determine how much depth is warranted while also adapting regularization.

The model places a beta process over hidden layers, allowing an unbounded number of layers in its formulation. This process induces layer-specific activation probabilities. A related Bernoulli process produces binary vectors that control neuron activation. These linked components make depth selection and dropout parts of one probabilistic model rather than independent choices.

Experiments across domains report better performance than state-of-the-art methods together with well-calibrated uncertainty estimates. In continual learning, the network can change its depth as additional data arrives, extending beyond its initial structure. The authors also report alleviation of catastrophic forgetting. The findings connect adaptive model structure to predictive performance, uncertainty quality, and the ability to accommodate incrementally available information.
neurips-2021-joint-inference-for-neural-.tldr: A unified Bayesian model adapts network depth and dropout to data, with reported benefits for performance, uncertainty, and continual learning.

paragraphs: Video question answering often trains on each clip-text pair independently. This paper argues that clips from the same video contain related visual and semantic information that can help one another. Its Siamese Sampling and Reasoning approach, SiaSamRea, brings those relationships into the model's reasoning and training guidance.

A sampling mechanism selects sparse, similar clips from a video. A knowledge-generation module then learns relationships among the clips. A second module propagates the relationship weights to the candidate predictions across clips, producing refined soft labels. These labels provide graded guidance drawn from the video's own related samples, allowing the model to learn from their interdependence.

The method achieves reported state-of-the-art performance on five VideoQA benchmarks. The stated gains are 2.1% on MSRVTT-QA, 2.9% on MSVD-QA, 1.0% on ActivityNet-QA, 1.8% on How2QA, and 4.3% on the action task of TGIF-QA. These results support the usefulness of sharing information among contextual clips instead of treating each clip-text training example as independent.
neurips-2021-learning-from-inside-self-d.tldr: SiaSamRea uses relationships among clips from the same video to refine training labels and improve video question answering.

paragraphs: Neural Trees change where a graph neural network performs message passing. Instead of operating directly on the input graph, the model uses a constructed tree called an H-tree. Each tree node represents an input subgraph, and its parent represents a larger subgraph, creating a hierarchy for processing graph structure.

The authors prove that this architecture can approximate any smooth probability distribution function over an undirected graph. The required parameter count is linear in graph size but exponential in treewidth, making structural complexity important to the bound. They also show that nonlinear combinations of these distribution functions can approximate continuous functions with the specified graph invariance or equivariance.

For semi-supervised node classification in 3D scene graphs, the paper reports significant prediction-accuracy gains over traditional GNN architectures. It also applies Neural Trees to citation networks with large treewidth using graph subsampling. The work links a hierarchical message-passing design to approximation guarantees and demonstrates practical benefits in the evaluated graph-learning tasks.
neurips-2021-neural-trees-for-learning-o.tldr: Neural Trees move message passing onto a hierarchy of subgraphs, providing approximation guarantees and improved scene-graph classification.

paragraphs: Learning image-goal navigation often relies on a simulator where a policy can interact with an environment and receive rewards derived from ground-truth maps. Building those simulators requires manual work for individual scenes. Differences between simulated and real environments also complicate transferring learned navigation policies to robots.

This paper asks whether those training requirements are necessary for the image-goal task. Its method, No RL, No Simulator, or NRNS, learns through a self-supervised approach using only passive videos of roaming. The training information therefore comes from recorded movement, without requiring the learning policy to actively collect interactions, access ground-truth maps, or train through reinforcement learning.

The authors describe NRNS as simple and scalable and report that it outperforms reinforcement-learning-based formulations by a significant margin. They propose it as a strong baseline for future image-based navigation research using RL or simulation. The finding establishes passive video learning as a competitive approach in the studied setting and challenges the assumed need for interactive simulator training.
neurips-2021-no-rl-no-simulation-learnin.tldr: NRNS learns image-goal navigation from passive roaming videos and reports substantial gains over reinforcement-learning-based approaches.

paragraphs: Adversarial training aims to make models less vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper examines its algorithmic stability: how sensitive a training procedure is to changes in its training data. Stability matters because it can help establish an upper bound on generalization error, connecting training behavior to performance beyond the observed samples.

The authors derive both upper and lower stability bounds for a generic adversarial training algorithm. Their analysis attributes worse stability than ordinary training to nondifferentiability in adversarial training. The issue is therefore not just how low the training loss becomes, but how the mathematical behavior of the objective affects sensitivity during learning.

To address this problem, the paper considers injecting noise. The analysis shows that noise allows the training trajectory to avoid nondifferentiability with dominating probability, improving stability. It also examines how stability relates to numerical errors when adversarial attacks are approximated. Together, these results connect generalization analysis to both the objective's irregularities and the computational approximation used during training.
neurips-2021-on-the-algorithmic-stabilit.tldr: The paper links weaker stability in adversarial training to nondifferentiability and analyzes noise injection as a remedy.

paragraphs: Online anomaly detection repeatedly decides whether each new observation is normal or unusual. Treating those decisions as statistical tests creates a need to control false discoveries across the sequence. This paper proposes false discovery rate control rules designed specifically for that ongoing time-series setting.

In each test, normality is the null hypothesis and an anomaly is the alternative. Controlling false discoveries lets users target a lower bound on precision in an unsupervised setting: it connects the testing procedure to the reliability of the anomalies it flags. The paper focuses on keeping detection power high while providing that control.

Two conditions make this difficult in practice: genuine anomalies may be extremely rare, and nearby test statistics may depend on one another. The proposed rules address shortcomings of previous methods under these characteristic conditions. The authors support the rules with theoretical results and experiments. Their contribution is therefore a testing framework tailored to detecting rare events in dependent streams while managing the reliability of reported detections.
neurips-2021-online-false-discovery-rate.tldr: The paper designs online false discovery controls that retain detection power for rare anomalies in serially dependent time series.

paragraphs: An image may contain much more detail than a person needs to make a particular decision. This paper trains image compression around preserving the user's actions. Its objective is for a person viewing a compressed image to act as they would after viewing the original, while transmitting fewer bits.

Training includes humans performing tasks with compressed images. A discriminator learns to distinguish whether an action followed an original or compressed image, providing an approximation to the compression model's loss. This makes user behavior part of the training signal and allows the retained visual information to adapt to the task.

Experiments cover handwritten-digit reading, face-photo verification, shopping-catalogue browsing, and a racing game. The method matches actions at lower bitrates than baselines. Its outputs preserve task-relevant properties: digit identity despite changed handwriting, hats and glasses despite randomized faces, perceived price despite changed colors and backgrounds, and upcoming road bends. These examples show how behavior-based compression can prioritize different information for different uses.
neurips-2021-pragmatic-image-compression.tldr: Human-in-the-loop compression learns which visual information preserves users' decisions, matching actions at lower bitrates than baselines.

paragraphs: Feature attribution methods produce maps intended to explain which parts of an input matter to a model's decision. Although people are often the intended users, these methods are commonly assessed with automatic proxy scores. This paper directly studies whether attribution maps help people perform image-classification tasks with AI assistance.

The user study covers ImageNet classification and fine-grained dog classification using Stanford Dogs, including natural images and images with adversarial perturbations. Overall, attribution maps are no more effective than showing nearby examples from the training set. On the harder dog-categorization task, human-AI teams shown attribution maps perform worse than the AI alone.

The authors also find poor correlation between automatic attribution-map evaluation measures and actual human-AI team performance. A favorable proxy score therefore does not reliably track the practical benefit measured in these studies. The findings motivate evaluating explanations in their intended human-in-the-loop applications and reconsidering existing automatic metrics, rather than assuming that an explanation's score establishes its usefulness to people.
neurips-2021-the-effectiveness-of-featur.tldr: User studies find limited benefits from attribution maps and poor agreement between automatic explanation scores and human-AI performance.

paragraphs: The lottery ticket hypothesis concerns sparse subnetworks that can train successfully in isolation. Finding these winning tickets with iterative magnitude-based pruning is computationally expensive, especially when the process must be repeated for each architecture. This paper asks whether a ticket found in one network can be transformed for another.

The authors investigate strategies for adapting tickets between networks in the same model family, such as ResNets. Their Elastic Lottery Ticket Hypothesis proposes that carefully replicating or dropping layers, and changing their order, can stretch or compress a ticket to suit a deeper or shallower network. The goal is performance nearly as competitive as a ticket discovered directly for the destination network.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet motivate the hypothesis. The paper also compares the approach with pruning-at-initialization and dynamic sparse training methods, and discusses transfer across model families, layer types, and datasets. The central finding supports reusing sparse structures within model families as a way to reduce repeated ticket-search costs.
neurips-2021-the-elastic-lottery-ticket-.tldr: Winning sparse subnetworks can be adapted across depths within a model family, potentially avoiding repeated expensive pruning searches.

paragraphs: A seller learning prices from purchase responses faces a strategic problem: the buyer can shape those responses to influence future prices. This paper analyzes a manipulation strategy in which the buyer commits, before interaction begins, to act as though they had a different value function.

The authors fully characterize the best value function for the buyer to imitate within this strategy, together with the resulting seller revenue and buyer surplus. This makes the consequences of manipulation explicit. The buyer's observed responses reflect a chosen imitation, so the seller's learning process operates on strategically shaped evidence.

The equilibrium characterizations depend strongly on production costs. With concave production costs, seller revenue is essentially zero. With convex costs, it is expressed through the Bregman divergence of the cost function between no production and a specified production level. The paper also shows that a more powerful class of pricing schemes need not improve revenue and can harm it. These results identify limits to the seller's gains from pricing flexibility under the studied manipulation.
neurips-2021-the-limits-of-optimal-prici.tldr: The paper characterizes strategic buyer imitation and shows that greater pricing flexibility can sometimes reduce seller revenue.

paragraphs: Language GANs face a training difficulty because words are discrete. In the setting described by this paper, the generator learns through reinforcement-learning rewards from a discriminator, rather than direct gradient flow through continuous outputs. This can make learning highly unstable.

The proposed SelfGAN framework has the generator and discriminator cooperate when producing training sequences. Those cooperative sequences are constructed to receive higher discriminator scores. The authors argue that this provides denser rewards to guide generator training. It also produces a more compact artificial training set for the discriminator, improving its accuracy and stability.

The same cooperation thus affects both sides of the training process: the generator receives richer guidance, while the discriminator learns from a more focused set of generated outputs. Experiments report that SelfGAN outperforms teacher forcing and achieves state-of-the-art results on summarization and question generation. These results support cooperative sequence production as a useful approach to the instability encountered in the language-GAN training setting studied.
neurips-2021-to-beam-or-not-to-beam-that.tldr: SelfGAN makes generators and discriminators cooperate on training sequences, improving learning guidance and reported language-generation results.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether conditional mutual information, or CMI, can unify generalization analysis in the realizable setting. It first obtains nontrivial but suboptimal bounds for algorithms whose outputs belong to classes with bounded VC dimension. It then asks when CMI gives optimal bounds or handles unrestricted output classes.

The authors prove that stable compression schemes of size k have CMI bounded on the order of k, yielding an optimal expected-risk bound for support vector machines learning halfspaces. They also identify an obstruction to constant-CMI proper learning. For a separate question, they show that outputting all classifiers consistent with the data has bounded CMI exactly when the hypothesis class has bounded star number.

The framework can also express leave-one-out analysis, extending its reach beyond restrictions on output classes. Its broadest equivalence concerns every consistent algorithm and data distribution: expected risk vanishes with increasing sample size if and only if evaluated CMI grows sublinearly. This establishes a precise universality claim while preserving consistency and the evaluated form of CMI as essential qualifiers.
neurips-2021-towards-a-unified-informati.tldr: The paper establishes broad generalization results through conditional mutual information while identifying precise conditions and limits on its bounds.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows transform a simple distribution into a more complex one while keeping density evaluation tractable. Standard flows cannot directly represent data supported on an unknown lower-dimensional manifold. This matters when the data occupies a lower-dimensional structure inside its larger observation space, as can occur with images.

Previous attempts to address this setting introduce geometric complications that undermine exact density evaluation. This paper proposes Conformal Embedding Flows to learn the manifold while retaining tractable densities. Its construction combines a standard flow with a trainable conformal embedding, giving the model a way to represent both a distribution and the structure on which it lies.

The authors present conformal building blocks for constructing these models and test them on synthetic and real-world data. The experiments demonstrate modeling of manifold-supported distributions without giving up tractable likelihoods. The contribution brings manifold learning and density estimation together in a flow framework, preserving a central computational benefit that earlier manifold-oriented adaptations had made difficult to retain.
neurips-2021-tractable-density-estimatio.tldr: Conformal Embedding Flows learn lower-dimensional data manifolds while retaining tractable density evaluation.

paragraphs: When a training dataset links a target label to a biased feature, a classifier can learn to rely on that association. Its predictions can then fail when the association changes. This paper proposes training methods aimed at reducing that reliance, covering datasets both with and without explicit bias labels.

Bias-Contrastive loss uses known bias labels within a contrastive-learning framework. Bias-Balanced regression trains the classifier toward a distribution with balanced relationships between targets and biases. These approaches use information about the bias to change the learning objective, addressing the correlation that could otherwise become a shortcut for prediction.

For datasets without bias labels, Soft Bias-Contrastive loss replaces the pair assignments used by BiasCon with softened assignments. It derives these from distances in the feature space of a model that captures bias. Experiments report significant improvements over previous debiasing methods on several realistic datasets. The contribution provides related training objectives for different levels of available bias information, with empirical evidence that they improve classification under the evaluated conditions.
neurips-2021-unbiased-classification-thr.tldr: The paper introduces contrastive and balancing objectives that reduce classifiers' reliance on biased correlations, with or without bias labels.

paragraphs: This paper develops planning and learning algorithms by examining design choices in earlier width-based planners. The work concerns lookahead methods with learned base policies and heuristics, evaluated on Atari-2600 games. Its strongest reported method is Novelty guided Critical Path Learning, abbreviated N-CPL.

The authors report that N-CPL outperforms the earlier width-based approaches pi-IW(1), pi-IW(1)+, and pi-HIW(n, 1). They also organize Atari games into a taxonomy based on defining characteristics. This adds an explanatory dimension to the evaluation: the comparisons can be examined in relation to the kinds of decision problems the games present.

The analysis highlights games with large branching factors and games where meaningful rewards are sparse. Large branching factors involve many possible continuations, while sparse meaningful rewards provide infrequent useful feedback. N-CPL outperforms the named prior approaches in these categories. The paper therefore contributes both improved algorithms within the evaluated planning family and a characterization of game properties that helps interpret their behavior and performance.
neurips-2021-width-based-lookaheads-with.tldr: N-CPL improves on earlier width-based Atari planners, with a game taxonomy clarifying performance in branching and sparse-reward settings.
